newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: Private cash for S.Africa's new-look safari parks.
newsitem.headline: Private cash for S.Africa's new-look safari parks.

text.p: Custodians of South Africa's top wildlife region announced a major commercial partnership on Thursday.
The Mpumalanga Parks Board launched a joint venture company with the Dubai-based Dolphin Group to capitalise on the region's nature reserves, mountain vistas and dry landscape.

Under the union between the state parks board and Dolphin, a major player in Africa's leisure industry through its Block Hotels and United Touring Company, the multinational takes over commercial running of the board's tourism and marketing divisions.
The investment is expected to be around 400 million rand ($87.5 million).

A primary objective of the joint venture is to ensure that South Africa's newest park authority can become self-sufficient despite progressively dwindling state funding, and at the same time preserve the region's rich natural heritage.
It plans to build tourist accommodation totalling 2,000 beds with theme camps and lodges and various adventure activities, in addition to traditional game viewing.

Mpumalanga has a population of three million people, some of whom are extremely poor. The province has the second lowest literacy rate in the country, while the population growth rate is higher than the national average.
During the last decade, jobs have dried up.

New developments will centre on the historic miners' town of Pilgrim's Rest, the majestic Blyde river canyon -- a massive red sandstone gorge with cliff faces plunging 700 metres in parts -- and the Loskop dam reserve.
The initial project envisages four years of construction, with resultant spinoffs for the local building and service industries.
Parks Board chief executive Alan Gray said in a prepared statement that without private sector intervention, conservation in the province would face an uncertain future.
"It is inappropriate to play the purist when considering the region's development pressures," Gray said.
"The future, we believe, lies in cooperation where the benefits derived from tourism can be shared by developers, the parks board and the community in a...permanent partnership."

The country's premier tourist attraction, the Kruger National Park covering 20,000 sq km (7,700 sq miles) of natural African bush, falls partially within Mpumalanga and while not included in the deal, it draws 700,000 tourists annually.
Kruger is the world-renowned magnet which should help attract new safari tourists to the development.

Mpumalanga, despite its tourist potential, is cash-strapped. President Nelson Mandela's 2-1/2-year-old democratic government has reduced subsidies to the parks and is pressing wildlife authorities to create jobs for blacks.

Confronted with similar demands, the neighbouring Natal Parks Board announced last month it was considering linking up with the privately owned Conservation Corporation to list the Greater St Lucia wetlands, Africa's largest system of estuaries, on the Johannesburg Stock Exchange.
